holidays.name: National Eggnog Day
holidays.description: Raise a mug of creamy, nutmeg-dusted holiday goodness. Whether you like your eggnog spiked, chilled, homemade, or straight from the carton, December 24 is the day to toast this rich and polarizing seasonal sip.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food observance that falls on Christmas Eve, when eggnog is traditionally at its peak popularity. Eggnog itself traces back to medieval Britain, where a milk-and-egg drink called posset was enjoyed, and the American colonies later swapped in rum.
holidays.funFact: In 1826, a riot broke out at West Point over eggnog. Cadets smuggled in whiskey to spike the holiday batch, and the 'Eggnog Riot' ended with around 20 cadets facing discipline or dismissal.

holidays.name: Christmas Book Flood (Jólabókaflóðið)
holidays.description: An Icelandic tradition where families exchange books on Christmas Eve, then spend the night reading them, often with hot chocolate and chocolate treats. It's a cozy holiday for bookworms.
holidays.origin: The tradition grew out of World War II-era Iceland. Imports were tightly restricted, but paper was relatively cheap, so books became the go-to gift. Publishers now release most of their new titles in the months before Christmas.
holidays.funFact: Iceland's publishers send a free catalog of new books, called the Bókatíðindi, to every household in the country each year, so everyone can choose their holiday reading.

holidays.name: National Re-gifting Day
holidays.description: A day to admit that the fruitcake you got last year might make someone else's holiday. Re-gifting Day celebrates passing along unused presents, with the unofficial rule being to double-check who gave it to you first.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance of unclear origin, popular as a last-minute-gifting joke on Christmas Eve.
holidays.funFact: The word 'regifting' got a big boost from a 1998 episode of Seinfeld, in which Elaine's boyfriend is accused of passing along a label maker.
